items.stem: Which equation does NOT apply to uniformly accelerated motion in a straight line?
items.answer: s = vt²
items.markingKey: The suvat equations are v = u + at, s = ½(u + v)t, s = ut + ½at², v² = u² + 2as.

items.stem: Starting from the definition of acceleration, derive v = u + at.
items.answer: a = (v − u)/t for uniform acceleration; rearranging gives v − u = at, so v = u + at.
items.markingKey: a = (v − u)/t [1]; rearrangement [1] [2]

items.stem: Use a velocity-time graph to derive s = ut + ½at².
items.answer: The area under the line from u to v in time t is a rectangle ut plus a triangle ½(v − u)t; since v − u = at, s = ut + ½at².
items.markingKey: area = rectangle + triangle [1]; substitute v − u = at [1] [2]

items.stem: A tram approaches a platform and decelerates uniformly from 20 m s⁻¹ at 2.5 m s⁻² for 6.0 s. Work out the displacement in this time.
items.markingKey: s = ut + ½at² = 20 × 6.0 + ½ × −2.5 × 6.0² = 75 m. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A cyclist rides down a hill and accelerates uniformly from 4.0 m s⁻¹ to 19 m s⁻¹ over a distance of 57.5 m. Calculate the magnitude of the acceleration.
items.answer: 3.0 m s⁻²
items.markingKey: a = (v² − u²)/(2s) = (19² − 4.0²)/(2 × 57.5) = 3.0 m s⁻². (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [3]

items.stem: A lorry approaches traffic lights and decelerates uniformly from 15 m s⁻¹ at 3.0 m s⁻² for 4.0 s. (a) Calculate the final velocity. (b) Calculate the displacement. (c) Calculate the average velocity and show it equals ½(u + v).
items.markingKey: (a) v = u + at [1] = 3.0 m s⁻¹ [1] (b) s = ut + ½at² = 36 m [1] (c) s/t = 9.0 m s⁻¹ and ½(u + v) = 9.0 m s⁻¹ [1] [4]

items.stem: A rocket sled starts at 5.0 m s⁻¹ and accelerates uniformly at 1.5 m s⁻² for 8.0 s. It then decelerates uniformly at 4.0 m s⁻² to rest. (a) Calculate the maximum speed. (b) Calculate the braking distance.
items.markingKey: (a) v = u + at (method/substitution) [1]; answer 17 m s⁻¹ with unit [1] [2] (b) s = v²/(2a) (method/substitution) [1]; answer 36.1 m with unit [1] [2]

items.stem: A rocket sled starts at 3.0 m s⁻¹ and accelerates uniformly at 2.5 m s⁻² for 6.0 s. It then decelerates uniformly at 3.0 m s⁻² to rest. (a) Calculate the total time from start to stop. (b) State the assumption made in using the equations of uniformly accelerated motion. (c) Sketch the velocity-time graph for the whole motion.
items.answer: (a) 12 s (b) The acceleration is constant during each stage (and motion is in a straight line). (c) Straight line rising from u to the maximum speed, then a steeper straight line falling to zero.
items.markingKey: (a) braking time = 18/3.0 = 6.0 s, add 6.0 s (method/substitution) [1]; answer 12 s with unit [1] [2] (b) The acceleration is constant during each stage (and motion is in a straight line) [1] (c) rising line [1]; falling line steeper/shallower as appropriate to zero [1] [2]

items.stem: A car accelerates uniformly from rest at 2.0 m s⁻² for 5.0 s. How far does it travel?
A train slows uniformly from 30 m s⁻¹ to rest in 600 m. What is the deceleration?
The equations of uniformly accelerated motion can only be used when …
items.answer: the acceleration is constant
items.markingKey: They are derived assuming constant acceleration in a straight line.

items.stem: Derive v² = u² + 2as from s = ½(u + v)t and v = u + at.
items.answer: From v = u + at, t = (v − u)/a. Substitute: s = ½(u + v)(v − u)/a = (v² − u²)/(2a), so v² = u² + 2as.
items.markingKey: eliminate t [1]; algebra to v² = u² + 2as [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the equations of uniformly accelerated motion cannot be used for a skydiver from the moment of leaving the aircraft until opening the parachute.
items.answer: Air resistance increases with speed, so the resultant force and acceleration decrease; the acceleration is not constant.
items.markingKey: air resistance varies with speed [1]; acceleration not constant [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why s = ut + ½at² can give two positive values of t for a given displacement s.
items.answer: If the acceleration is opposite to u, the object passes the position s twice: once on the way out and once on the way back.
items.markingKey: acceleration opposite to velocity [1]; passes the point twice [1] [2]

items.stem: Leila calculates the distance travelled by a car that accelerates uniformly from 10 m s⁻¹ at 2.0 m s⁻² for 5.0 s and writes "s = ut + at² = 100 m". Identify the error and give the correct distance. Explain how a velocity-time graph supports the correct equation.
items.answer: The factor ½ is missing: s = ut + ½at² = 75 m. On the v-t graph the area above the rectangle ut is a triangle of area ½ × t × at.
items.markingKey: missing ½ identified [1]; correct value [1]; triangle area ½t(at) [1] [3]

items.stem: Ines is driving at 25 m s⁻¹ on a road near Lisbon when a hazard appears. Reaction time is 0.80 s and the brakes then give a uniform deceleration of 7.0 m s⁻². Calculate the braking distance.
items.markingKey: v² = u² + 2as → s = u²/(2a) = 25²/(2 × 7.0) = 44.6 m. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A lorry approaches traffic lights and decelerates uniformly from 25 m s⁻¹ at 1.5 m s⁻² for 5.0 s. Calculate the final velocity.
items.markingKey: v = u + at = 25 + (−1.5)(5.0) = 17.5 m s⁻¹. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Nadia is driving at 31.3 m s⁻¹ on a road near Accra when a hazard appears. Reaction time is 1.2 s and the brakes then give a uniform deceleration of 6.0 m s⁻². Calculate the braking distance.
items.markingKey: v² = u² + 2as → s = u²/(2a) = 31.3²/(2 × 6.0) = 81.6 m. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Omar is driving at 25 m s⁻¹ on a road near Mumbai when a hazard appears. Reaction time is 0.70 s and the brakes then give a uniform deceleration of 6.0 m s⁻². Calculate the total stopping distance.
items.markingKey: thinking distance = 25 × 0.70 = 17.5 m [1]; braking = u²/2a = 52.1 m [1]; total 69.6 m [1] [3]

items.stem: A car joins a motorway and accelerates uniformly from 10 m s⁻¹ at 2.0 m s⁻² for 5.0 s. (a) Calculate the final velocity. (b) Calculate the displacement. (c) Calculate the average velocity and show it equals ½(u + v).
items.markingKey: (a) v = u + at [1] = 20 m s⁻¹ [1] (b) s = ut + ½at² = 75 m [1] (c) s/t = 15 m s⁻¹ and ½(u + v) = 15 m s⁻¹ [1]; valid because acceleration is uniform [1] [5]

items.stem: A test car on a track in Dhaka accelerates uniformly from 3.0 m s⁻¹ at 2.0 m s⁻² for 10 s, then brakes with a uniform deceleration of 3.0 m s⁻² until it stops. (a) Calculate the distance travelled while accelerating. (b) State the assumption made in using the equations of uniformly accelerated motion.
items.answer: (a) 130 m (b) The acceleration is constant during each stage (and motion is in a straight line).
items.markingKey: (a) s = ut + ½at² (method/substitution) [1]; answer 130 m with unit [1] [2] (b) The acceleration is constant during each stage (and motion is in a straight line) [1]

items.stem: A rocket sled starts at 5.0 m s⁻¹ and accelerates uniformly at 2.5 m s⁻² for 8.0 s. It then decelerates uniformly at 5.0 m s⁻² to rest. (a) Calculate the maximum speed. (b) Calculate the total time from start to stop.
items.answer: (a) 25 m s⁻¹ (b) 13 s
items.markingKey: (a) v = u + at (method/substitution) [1]; answer 25 m s⁻¹ with unit [1] [2] (b) braking time = 25/5.0 = 5.0 s, add 8.0 s (method/substitution) [1]; answer 13 s with unit [1] [2]

items.stem: A ball is thrown vertically upwards. Ignoring air resistance, what is its acceleration at the highest point?
options: It depends on the speed of throw
items.answer: 9.81 m s⁻² downwards
items.markingKey: The only force is weight; a = g downwards throughout the flight.

items.stem: Explain why a skydiver falling from rest reaches a terminal velocity.
items.answer: As speed increases, air resistance increases; the resultant force (weight − drag) and so the acceleration decrease until drag equals weight; then the acceleration is zero and speed is constant.
items.markingKey: drag increases with speed [1]; resultant force decreases to zero [1]; constant (terminal) velocity [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why a skydiver slows down when the parachute opens.
items.answer: The larger area greatly increases air resistance so drag exceeds weight; the resultant force is upwards, causing deceleration until a new, lower terminal velocity is reached.
items.markingKey: drag increases (larger area) [1]; drag > weight so deceleration [1]; lower terminal velocity [1] [3]

items.stem: A coin is projected vertically upwards at 12 m s⁻¹. Air resistance is negligible. Work out the time taken to reach maximum height.
items.markingKey: t = u/g = 12/9.81 = 1.22 s. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A tennis ball is projected vertically upwards at 18 m s⁻¹. Air resistance is negligible. Calculate the maximum height and the total time before it returns to the point of projection.

A skydiver of mass 60 kg jumps from a hovering helicopter above Santiago. She reaches a terminal velocity of 60 m s⁻¹ before opening her parachute, after which her new terminal velocity is 5 m s⁻¹. (a) State the acceleration at the instant of leaving the helicopter, giving a reason. (b) Explain why the skydiver decelerates when the parachute opens.
items.answer: (a) 9.81 m s⁻²: the speed is zero so there is no air resistance; only weight acts. (b) Drag increases suddenly (larger area) above the weight; resultant force upwards causes deceleration.
items.markingKey: (a) g [1]; no drag at zero speed [1] [2] (b) drag > weight [1]; resultant upwards [1] [2]

items.stem: A stone is dropped from rest. Ignoring air resistance, what is its speed after 2.0 s?
Describe the velocity-time graph for a ball thrown vertically upwards and caught at the same level, ignoring air resistance.
items.answer: A straight line of constant negative gradient (−g), crossing the time axis at the top of the flight; the final velocity is equal in magnitude and opposite in direction to the initial velocity.
items.markingKey: straight line gradient −g [1]; crosses axis at top; symmetrical [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain how air resistance changes the velocity-time graph of a falling ball.
items.answer: The gradient starts at g but decreases as speed increases (curve that flattens), approaching a constant terminal velocity.
items.markingKey: gradient decreases [1]; levels off at terminal velocity [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the acceleration of a falling object is independent of its mass when air resistance is negligible.
items.answer: a = F/m = mg/m = g; both the weight and the inertia are proportional to mass.
items.markingKey: weight ∝ m [1]; a = mg/m = g [1] [2]

items.stem: A steel ball bearing and a table-tennis ball are released together from a height of 5.0 m in air. Explain whether they reach the ground at the same time, and what would happen in a vacuum.
items.answer: In air the object with the greater weight compared with its air resistance (larger mass per unit area) has the greater acceleration and lands first; in a vacuum both fall with acceleration g and land together.
items.markingKey: air resistance relative to weight decides acceleration [1]; correct object lands first [1]; vacuum: same acceleration g [1] [3]

items.stem: A stone falls from rest down a well through a height of 30 m. Air resistance is negligible. Calculate the time of fall.
items.markingKey: t = √(2h/g) = √(2 × 30/9.81) = 2.47 s. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A ball is dropped from a balcony. The sound of it landing is heard 1.60 s after release. Taking the speed of sound as 330 m s⁻¹ and ignoring air resistance, show that the height is about 12 m.
items.answer: h = 12 m
items.markingKey: tfall + h/330 = 1.60 [1]; with tfall = √(2h/g), h = 12 m satisfies this (or trial values) [1]; check [1] [3]

items.stem: A stone is projected vertically upwards at 15 m s⁻¹. Air resistance is negligible. Calculate the maximum height and the total time before it returns to the point of projection.

A skydiver of total mass 75 kg falls from rest, reaching 60 m s⁻¹ terminal velocity; after the parachute opens the terminal velocity is 5 m s⁻¹. (a) State the acceleration at the instant of leaving the helicopter, giving a reason. (b) Sketch the velocity-time graph from leaving the helicopter to landing.
items.answer: (a) 9.81 m s⁻²: the speed is zero so there is no air resistance; only weight acts. (b) curve rising with decreasing gradient to 60 m s⁻¹; sharp drop when parachute opens; curve levelling at 5 m s⁻¹
items.markingKey: (a) g [1]; no drag at zero speed [1] [2] (b) curve to first terminal velocity [1]; drop to lower terminal velocity [1] [2]

items.stem: A skydiver of mass 60 kg jumps from a hovering helicopter above Lisbon. She reaches a terminal velocity of 60 m s⁻¹ before opening her parachute, after which her new terminal velocity is 5 m s⁻¹. (a) Calculate the weight of the skydiver. (b) State the acceleration at the instant of leaving the helicopter, giving a reason. (c) State the air resistance at terminal velocity. (d) Explain why the skydiver decelerates when the parachute opens.
items.answer: (a) 589 N (b) 9.81 m s⁻²: the speed is zero so there is no air resistance; only weight acts. (c) 589 N (equal to weight) (d) Drag increases suddenly (larger area) above the weight; resultant force upwards causes deceleration.
items.markingKey: (a) W = mg: 589 N [1] (b) g [1]; no drag at zero speed [1] [2] (c) equal to weight: 589 N (equal to weight) [1] (d) drag > weight [1]; resultant upwards [1] [2]

items.stem: A ball is thrown horizontally from a cliff. Ignoring air resistance, which quantity stays constant during its flight?
items.answer: The horizontal component of velocity
items.markingKey: No horizontal force acts, so horizontal velocity is constant.

items.stem: Explain why the path of a projectile is curved.
items.answer: The horizontal velocity is constant but the vertical velocity increases uniformly downwards due to g, so the direction of motion continuously changes.
items.markingKey: constant horizontal velocity [1]; vertical velocity changes due to g [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain how air resistance affects the range and maximum height of a projectile.
items.answer: Air resistance opposes the motion, reducing both components of velocity; the maximum height and the range are both reduced and the path is no longer symmetrical (steeper descent).
items.markingKey: both reduced [1]; path asymmetric/steeper descent [1] [2]

items.stem: A dart is thrown horizontally at 25 m s⁻¹ from a height of 1.8 m above level ground. Air resistance is negligible. Calculate the time taken to reach the ground.
items.markingKey: h = ½gt² → t = √(2 × 1.8/9.81) = 0.606 s. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A parcel is released from a drone moving horizontally at 3.0 m s⁻¹ from a height of 1.2 m above level ground. Air resistance is negligible. Calculate the horizontal distance travelled before it hits the ground.
items.markingKey: t = √(2h/g) = 0.495 s [1]; horizontal velocity constant [1]; x = ut = 1.48 m [1] [3]

items.stem: A ball rolls off a horizontal table at 8.0 m s⁻¹ from a height of 45 m above level ground. Air resistance is negligible. (a) Calculate the horizontal distance travelled. (b) Calculate the speed and the angle below the horizontal at which it hits the ground.
items.answer: (a) 24.2 m (b) 30.8 m s⁻¹ at 74.9° below the horizontal

items.stem: An athlete in Dubai releases a shot at a height of 2.0 m above level ground with a speed of 22 m s⁻¹ at 40° above the horizontal. (a) Calculate the time of flight. (b) State the speed of the projectile at its highest point.
items.markingKey: (a) −2.0 = 14.1t − 4.905t² solved (equation) [1]; substitution [1]; answer 3.02 s with unit [1] [3] (b) vertical component zero; speed = horizontal component [1]

items.stem: A ball is thrown from a height of 1.5 m above level ground at 20 m s⁻¹ and 40° above the horizontal by Mei. (a) Calculate the time of flight. (b) Explain how the range would change if air resistance were significant.
items.answer: (a) 2.73 s (b) The range would be smaller because air resistance reduces the horizontal velocity (and the height reached).

items.stem: Two balls are released at the same time from the same height: one is dropped and the other is projected horizontally. Ignoring air resistance, …
options: the faster ball has a greater vertical acceleration
they hit the ground at the same time
items.answer: they hit the ground at the same time

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) At the highest point of the path of a projectile (no air resistance), which is correct? (b) A projectile is launched at 20 m s⁻¹ at 30° above the horizontal. What is the initial vertical component of velocity?
items.answer: (a) The vertical velocity is zero and the acceleration is g downwards (b) 10 m s⁻¹
items.markingKey: (a) At the top v_y = 0 but the horizontal velocity and the acceleration g remain. (b) u sin θ = 20 × sin 30° = 10 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Explain why a bullet fired horizontally and one dropped from the same height at the same instant hit level ground together.
items.answer: Both have zero initial vertical velocity and the same vertical acceleration g, so they take the same time to fall the same height; horizontal velocity does not affect vertical motion.
items.markingKey: same initial vertical velocity (zero) and same g [1]; independence of components [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why launch angles of 30° and 60° give the same range on level ground (no air resistance).
items.answer: Range = u² sin 2θ / g and sin 60° = sin 120°, so both give the same range; the 60° launch goes higher and takes longer but moves more slowly horizontally.
items.markingKey: sin 2θ equal for complementary angles [1]; trade-off of time and horizontal speed [1] [2]

items.stem: Describe how the velocity of a projectile changes from launch to its highest point.
items.answer: The horizontal component is constant; the vertical component decreases uniformly to zero, so the speed decreases to a minimum (equal to the horizontal component) and the direction becomes horizontal.
items.markingKey: horizontal constant [1]; vertical decreases to zero; minimum speed at top [1] [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Describe how the velocity of a projectile changes from launch to its highest point. (b) Explain why launch angles of 30° and 60° give the same range on level ground (no air resistance).

(b) Range = u² sin 2θ / g and sin 60° = sin 120°, so both give the same range; the 60° launch goes higher and takes longer but moves more slowly horizontally.
items.markingKey: (a) horizontal constant [1]; vertical decreases to zero; minimum speed at top [1] [2] (b) sin 2θ equal for complementary angles [1]; trade-off of time and horizontal speed [1] [2]

items.stem: A skydiver of total mass 75 kg falls from rest, reaching 55 m s⁻¹ terminal velocity; after the parachute opens the terminal velocity is 7 m s⁻¹. (a) Calculate the weight of the skydiver. (b) State the air resistance at terminal velocity. (c) Sketch the velocity-time graph from leaving the helicopter to landing.
items.answer: (a) 736 N (b) 736 N (equal to weight) (c) curve rising with decreasing gradient to 55 m s⁻¹; sharp drop when parachute opens; curve levelling at 7 m s⁻¹

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) State why the horizontal and vertical motions of a projectile can be treated separately. (b) What is the shape of the path of a projectile when air resistance is negligible?
items.answer: (a) Perpendicular components are independent: the vertical force (weight) has no horizontal component. (b) A parabola
items.markingKey: (a) perpendicular components independent [1] (b) Constant horizontal velocity with uniform vertical acceleration gives a parabolic path.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Describe how the velocity of a projectile changes from launch to its highest point. (b) Explain why the path of a projectile is curved.
items.answer: (a) The horizontal component is constant; the vertical component decreases uniformly to zero, so the speed decreases to a minimum (equal to the horizontal component) and the direction becomes horizontal. (b) The horizontal velocity is constant but the vertical velocity increases uniformly downwards due to g, so the direction of motion continuously changes.
items.markingKey: (a) horizontal constant [1]; vertical decreases to zero; minimum speed at top [1] [2] (b) constant horizontal velocity [1]; vertical velocity changes due to g [1] [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why the path of a projectile is curved. (b) Explain why a bullet fired horizontally and one dropped from the same height at the same instant hit level ground together.
items.answer: (a) The horizontal velocity is constant but the vertical velocity increases uniformly downwards due to g, so the direction of motion continuously changes. (b) Both have zero initial vertical velocity and the same vertical acceleration g, so they take the same time to fall the same height; horizontal velocity does not affect vertical motion.
items.markingKey: (a) constant horizontal velocity [1]; vertical velocity changes due to g [1] [2] (b) same initial vertical velocity (zero) and same g [1]; independence of components [1] [2]

items.stem: A ball rolls off a horizontal table at 5.0 m s⁻¹ from a height of 10 m above level ground. Air resistance is negligible. Determine the time taken to reach the ground.
items.markingKey: h = ½gt² → t = √(2 × 10/9.81) = 1.43 s. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A shot is put from ground level at 12 m s⁻¹ at 50° above the horizontal. Air resistance is negligible and the ground is level. Calculate the horizontal and vertical components of the initial velocity.

items.stem: An athlete in Madrid releases a shot at a height of 2.5 m above level ground with a speed of 20 m s⁻¹ at 40° above the horizontal. (a) Calculate the time of flight. (b) Explain how the range would change if air resistance were significant.
items.answer: (a) 2.80 s (b) The range would be smaller because air resistance reduces the horizontal velocity (and the height reached).

items.stem: A cyclist moving at 4.0 m s⁻¹ accelerates at 0.50 m s⁻² for 6.0 s. What is the final velocity?
items.answer: 7.0 m s⁻¹

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Starting from the definition of acceleration, derive v = u + at. (b) Use a velocity-time graph to derive s = ut + ½at².
items.answer: (a) a = (v − u)/t for uniform acceleration; rearranging gives v − u = at, so v = u + at. (b) The area under the line from u to v in time t is a rectangle ut plus a triangle ½(v − u)t; since v − u = at, s = ut + ½at².
items.markingKey: (a) a = (v − u)/t [1]; rearrangement [1] [2] (b) area = rectangle + triangle [1]; substitute v − u = at [1] [2]

items.stem: Arjun calculates the distance travelled by a car that accelerates uniformly from 5.0 m s⁻¹ at 3.0 m s⁻² for 5.0 s and writes "s = ut + at² = 100 m". Identify the error and give the correct distance. Explain how a velocity-time graph supports the correct equation.
items.answer: The factor ½ is missing: s = ut + ½at² = 62.5 m. On the v-t graph the area above the rectangle ut is a triangle of area ½ × t × at.
items.markingKey: missing ½ identified [1]; correct value [1]; triangle area ½t(at) [1] [3]

items.stem: A car joins a motorway and accelerates uniformly from 10 m s⁻¹ to 19 m s⁻¹ over a distance of 87 m. Work out the magnitude of the acceleration.
items.answer: 1.5 m s⁻²
items.markingKey: a = (v² − u²)/(2s) = (19² − 10²)/(2 × 87) = 1.5 m s⁻². (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Ines is driving at 20 m s⁻¹ on a road near Doha when a hazard appears. Reaction time is 0.60 s and the brakes then give a uniform deceleration of 5.0 m s⁻². Calculate the braking distance.
items.markingKey: v² = u² + 2as → s = u²/(2a) = 20²/(2 × 5.0) = 40 m. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Tomás is driving at 31.3 m s⁻¹ on a road near Muscat when a hazard appears. Reaction time is 1.0 s and the brakes then give a uniform deceleration of 7.5 m s⁻². Calculate the total stopping distance.

items.stem: A rocket sled starts at 3.0 m s⁻¹ and accelerates uniformly at 1.5 m s⁻² for 6.0 s. It then decelerates uniformly at 3.0 m s⁻² to rest. (a) Calculate the maximum speed. (b) Calculate the braking distance.

items.stem: A ball is thrown upwards at 15 m s⁻¹. Ignoring air resistance, how long does it take to reach its maximum height?
A crumpled ball of paper and a coin are released together from a height of 10 m in air. Explain whether they reach the ground at the same time, and what would happen in a vacuum.
items.answer: In air the object with the greater weight compared with its air resistance (larger mass per unit area) has the greater acceleration and lands first; in a vacuum both fall with acceleration g and land together.
items.markingKey: air resistance relative to weight decides acceleration [1]; correct object lands first [1]; vacuum: same acceleration g [1] [3]

items.stem: A skydiver of total mass 60 kg falls from rest, reaching 60 m s⁻¹ terminal velocity; after the parachute opens the terminal velocity is 6 m s⁻¹. (a) Explain why the skydiver decelerates when the parachute opens. (b) Sketch the velocity-time graph from leaving the helicopter to landing.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) A ball is thrown horizontally from a cliff. Ignoring air resistance, which quantity stays constant during its flight? (b) Ignoring air resistance, which launch angle gives the maximum range on level ground?
items.answer: (a) The horizontal component of velocity (b) 45°
items.markingKey: (a) No horizontal force acts, so horizontal velocity is constant. (b) R = u² sin 2θ/g is greatest when 2θ = 90°.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain how air resistance affects the range and maximum height of a projectile. (b) Explain why a bullet fired horizontally and one dropped from the same height at the same instant hit level ground together.
items.answer: (a) Air resistance opposes the motion, reducing both components of velocity; the maximum height and the range are both reduced and the path is no longer symmetrical (steeper descent). (b) Both have zero initial vertical velocity and the same vertical acceleration g, so they take the same time to fall the same height; horizontal velocity does not affect vertical motion.
items.markingKey: (a) both reduced [1]; path asymmetric/steeper descent [1] [2] (b) same initial vertical velocity (zero) and same g [1]; independence of components [1] [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Describe how the velocity of a projectile changes from launch to its highest point. (b) Explain why launch angles of 30° and 60° give the same range on level ground (no air resistance).
items.answer: (a) The horizontal component is constant; the vertical component decreases uniformly to zero, so the speed decreases to a minimum (equal to the horizontal component) and the direction becomes horizontal. (b) Range = u² sin 2θ / g and sin 60° = sin 120°, so both give the same range; the 60° launch goes higher and takes longer but moves more slowly horizontally.
items.markingKey: (a) horizontal constant [1]; vertical decreases to zero; minimum speed at top [1] [2] (b) sin 2θ equal for complementary angles [1]; trade-off of time and horizontal speed [1] [2]
